implementation_notes: The canonical Ruby realisation is the connection_pool gem (used by Sidekiq and many clients): ConnectionPool.new(size:, timeout:) { SomeClient.new } keeps the instances and .with { |conn| ... } checks one out, yields it and checks it back in even when the block raises, so the return path cannot be forgotten. Exhaustion raises ConnectionPool::TimeoutError after the timeout instead of hanging forever, a per-call timeout: override lets non-critical paths fail fast, and shutdown { |c| c.close } drains the pool when it is no longer needed. ActiveRecord owns a separate ConnectionPool for the same purpose; the gem's ::Wrapper (method_missing per-call checkout) exists only as a migration aid and is documented as not high-performance.
code_sketch:
$redis = ConnectionPool.new(size: 5, timeout: 5) { Redis.new }

$redis.with do |conn|        # checked out, yielded, checked back in
  conn.set('foo', 'bar')
end
pitfalls: Pools are per-process: a forked child inherits the parent's open sockets and its own copy of the pool, so re-create pools after fork or two processes will drive the same connection.
Manual checkout (pop/shift) loses the block's exception safety - prefer .with, or a stateful client will be returned dirty after a raise.
A slow operation inside .with occupies its instance for the whole duration; size the pool for the slowest common path or unrelated threads will hit TimeoutError.
